(i) The GREENLAB model of light interception in canopies can be extended to predict light interception in canopied plant communities, (ii) In the extended model, the light competition between plants is computed in terms of the light interception efficiency of the plants, and (iii) The extended model is capable of reproducing the observed effects of plant density on the light interception of individual plants, on the plant architecture, and on plant growth and yield.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the GREENLAB model is an attempt at a unified approach to plant architecture, growth and development, and the effects of the environment on these processes, with the aim of integrating the effects of the physical environment on the plant, and the effects that plant architecture has on resource capture and allocation.

we developed a new mathematical model of plant growth, the GREENLAB model, and we used it to study the effects of density and resource availability on resource acquisition and plant architectural development.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the GREENLAB model, which has been used to study plant development for over 15 years, is able to simulate the effects of density and light competition on the growth of a plant species.

the model is capable of simulating the effects of density and light availability on resource acquisition and plant architecture in a simple way, which is useful for understanding the mechanisms that control the growth of plants in the field and for developing new hypotheses about plant architecture and growth.
the GREENLAB model is able to reproduce a number of key features of the architecture of Arabidopsis thaliana plants growing under various light conditions.
